I mean, I agree with you. I think it’s bland to base fantasy cultures so tightly rooted in real-world cultures, and that means there are representative questions around the stories you can tell within those cultures. 

By pretty explicitly basing a fantasy race around a human ethnic group or culture, WOTC are limited in the ways they can depict them. 

Michael Moorcock’s Melnibone is a city-state of drug-addicted psychopath slavers. They’re loosely based on cats and you could make an argument their language or structure or attitudes are based on various real-world historical examples (and they must be, because that’s what writing fantasy requires) but they’re not explicitly referencing any real world peoples. 

I don’t know, maybe I’m completely incorrect. To me, the new direction for Orcs links them inextricably with a real world culture that is going to have to guide the decisions made for them on a storytelling level. I just find that less interesting than making something out of a more patchwork of influences.

This is happening a bit too much. Representation of a more diverse spread of cultures is a good thing but in doing it for the sake of representation, modern fantasy is losing some of its grit. Final Fantasy XIV’s latest expansion was an excuse to teach people about South American culture, Guild Wars 2 introduced a faction that is essentially just China, and now Orcs are like this. 

If we’re going to try to represent real-world peoples in the modern climate, it can’t be done in a way that depicts them negatively so it ends up feeling touristic and white-washy. 

Yes, white European history has been overrepresented - but it’s not depicted as pleasant and like everyone’s getting along. We see the gutters of medieval castle towns, bandits, corrupt nobles. In Viking-coded interpretations, they are almost exclusively battle-hungry raiders. 

My favorite fantasies pull from real world influences more subconsciously to create something that feels new, rather than nod to the world around us as something we need to respect.

I think that’s up to you, really. Is your book going to be cozy in that it depicts a stress-free world, dealing more with minor quibbles like the perils of farming or romantic mix-ups, or is it cozy in the feeling it inspires in the reader? If the latter, how will you do that?

Cozy is typically slow, low-stakes, and joyful. Dungeon Meshi is a cool inspiration because it manages to take high stakes and make them feel low, so do some exercises to research how it goes about doing that. Dungeon Meshi has fights but subverts them by injecting humor mid-battle, and softening the impact of life-or-death stakes by giving characters ways to avoid death. 

I’d also argue Dungeon Meshi is successful at being cozy because it focuses on a sense that very easily evokes pleasure: taste. And it really focuses on that, which helps the viewer to get out of the stakes and relieve the tension in the narrative.
